context: The queue is on the left and the vertical array is on the right. The label between them reads “Array implementation / Queue interface.” Both run from front to rear down the page. Moving down means increasing the index, just as moving right does in the discussion of a horizontal array that follows.
description: None of these three frames wraps past the end of the array. Here rear = front + size gives the next slot to write, just past the last element. The active indices form the closed interval [front, rear - 1]. Gray dashed cells and ellipses at both ends show the rest of the array. A slot leaving the active range does not imply that its old value has been cleared.

frames.announcement: The array-based queue starts as [1, 3, 2, 5], with size = 4. The front index points to the first element, 1, and rear points to the empty slot after the last element, 5.
frames.explanation: The queue starts as [1, 3, 2, 5], with size = 4. The orange front marker points to 1. The teal rear marker, calculated as front + 4, points to the first empty slot below 5. The callout explains that front marks the first element and rear is one past the index of the last.
frames.key_state: Initial queue: [1, 3, 2, 5], size = 4. The front index points to 1, and rear = front + size points to the empty slot below 5.
frames.title: Initial queue: locate the active range

frames.announcement: The call push(4) writes 4 at index rear and increases size to 5. The queue is now [1, 3, 2, 5, 4].
frames.explanation: The callout for push(4) lists three steps: calculate rear, insert the element at rear, and increment size by 1. Using the old size of 4 gives the empty slot below 5. Write the teal 4 there, then increase size to 5. The queue is now [1, 3, 2, 5, 4], and front still points to 1. The figure leaves rear at the slot where 4 was written. Recalculating it with the new size would place it at the empty slot immediately below 4.
frames.key_state: After push(4), the queue is [1, 3, 2, 5, 4], size = 5, and front points to 1. The figure shows rear at the slot where 4 was written.
frames.title: Enqueue 4 at index rear

frames.announcement: The call pop() moves front down to 3 and reduces size to 4. Element 1 leaves the queue, and the remaining elements [3, 2, 5, 4] stay in place.
frames.explanation: The call pop() removes and returns the old front element, 1. The callout says to increment front by 1 and decrement size by 1. The front marker moves down one slot to 3, and size drops from 5 to 4. The active queue is now [3, 2, 5, 4], with all four elements still in their original slots. A dashed outline marks the old slot for 1 as outside the active range. This frame has no rear marker.
frames.key_state: The call pop() returns 1. The front marker moves down one slot to 3, size = 4, and the active queue is [3, 2, 5, 4]. The slot that held 1 is outside the active range and has not been cleared. This frame omits rear.
frames.title: Advance front to dequeue 1

result: To enqueue, write the element at rear and increase size by 1. To dequeue, increase front by 1 and decrease size by 1. This avoids shifting the remaining elements on every dequeue, so both operations take O(1) time.
summary: The front index marks the first element, and size tracks the number of elements. Enqueueing writes to the slot just past the rear element. Dequeueing advances the front index and leaves the other elements in place.
title: Enqueueing and dequeueing with an array
